title: Interpreting Experimental Results
learning_outcomes: Explain interpreting experimental results and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of interpreting experimental results to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study interpreting experimental results in the context of statistical inference, experimentation, and causal analysis. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Interpreting Experimental Results matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: Visual overview: Interpreting Experimental Results
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 140: Interpreting Experimental Results; a three-stage visual for understanding the topic, applying it to a small example, and validating assumptions.
content_blocks.caption: Use the overview to connect interpreting experimental results to a concrete example and a responsible check.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Inference and experiments quantify uncertainty around comparisons. Statistical significance, causal identification, and practical value are distinct ideas.

items.title: Confidence intervals and effect sizes
items.text: Define confidence intervals and effect sizes in relation to interpreting experimental results; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Heterogeneous treatment effects
items.text: Work through heterogeneous treatment effects using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Practical implications
items.text: Check the edge cases for practical implications: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Experiment limitations
items.text: Document the rule or choice for experiment limitations so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Responsible recommendation-making
items.text: Define responsible recommendation-making in relation to interpreting experimental results; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by interpreting experimental results. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

p_value = 0.03
alpha = 0.05
print("statistically significant under threshold:", p_value < alpha)

For SQL, adapt the query to an approved local schema; the stated result is a conceptual query simulation, not a live database result.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. A p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true or the size of an effect.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Inference and experiments quantify uncertainty around comparisons. Statistical significance, causal identification, and practical value are distinct ideas. Next, connect this lesson to the linked prerequisite or following lesson. Record the method, input assumptions, observed result, and one limitation so another person can reproduce and review the work.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small synthetic example for interpreting experimental results. State a question, make a prediction, trace or run an appropriate calculation, then write one finding and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.
Record a reproducible example or a complete manual trace with an expected result.
Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
For SQL, use a local schema and read-only test data; this page does not provide a live database.
For package-dependent work, create an isolated environment and use the relevant official documentation.
